lessons.title: Foundations of Foreign Trade Negotiation in Africa
lessons.body: Foreign trade negotiation is the structured process by which buyers, sellers, agents, regulators, and logistics partners from different countries reach binding or non-binding agreements on the exchange of goods, services, or rights. In Africa, this process is shaped by a unique mix of opportunities and constraints: a young and growing consumer market, abundant natural resources, regional economic communities such as ECOWAS, SADC, EAC, COMESA, and the AfCFTA, but also infrastructure gaps, currency volatility, border delays, and information asymmetry. A practical negotiator must therefore combine commercial discipline with cultural intelligence and risk management. This lesson gives you the foundations you need before you sit at any table, whether in Lagos, Nairobi, Cairo, Johannesburg, or online with a buyer in Dubai or Guangzhou. The first foundation is clarity of objective. Before any negotiation, write a one-page mandate that states what you are selling or buying, the minimum acceptable outcome, the target outcome, the walk-away point, and the non-negotiables. For an African exporter of sesame from Ethiopia or shea butter from Ghana, the mandate might include price per metric ton, Incoterms, payment method, delivery window, quality specification, and dispute resolution forum. Without a written mandate, negotiators drift, concede too much, or accept terms that destroy margin. The second foundation is market intelligence. You need to know the reference price, the seasonality, the competitor offers, the tariff and non-tariff barriers, and the buyer profile. Use trade data from ITC Trade Map, UN Comtrade, national export promotion agencies, and industry associations. If you are importing machinery into Nigeria, check the HS code, duty rate, VAT, SONCAP requirements, and the current exchange rate regime. If you are exporting cocoa from Cote d Ivoire to the EU, check EUDR traceability requirements, farm-gate prices, and the London futures price. Intelligence turns a negotiation from a guessing game into a calculated exchange. The third foundation is understanding the structure of the deal. Foreign trade deals usually have six moving parts: product specification, price, delivery terms, payment terms, risk allocation, and relationship governance. Product specification covers quality, packaging, labeling, and certification. Price covers currency, unit price, price adjustment mechanisms, and volume discounts. Delivery terms cover Incoterms such as FOB, CIF, DAP, and the port or border point. Payment terms cover letters of credit, documentary collections, open account, advance payment, and now mobile money and fintech escrow. Risk allocation covers insurance, inspection, force majeure, sanctions, and currency hedging. Relationship governance covers communication, performance review, and dispute resolution. A skilled negotiator treats these as a package, not as isolated items. The fourth foundation is cultural and communication awareness. Africa is not one culture. Negotiation styles differ between North Africa, West Africa, East Africa, Central Africa, and Southern Africa, and between rural and urban, francophone, anglophone, lusophone, and arabophone business environments. In many African contexts, relationship building precedes transaction. Time may be polychronic, meaning several conversations and commitments happen at once. Direct confrontation may be avoided to preserve dignity, so a no may appear as we will study it or it is difficult. Silence can be a negotiating tool. Titles, age, and seniority matter. A practical negotiator learns to read indirect signals, to ask open questions, to confirm understanding in writing, and to avoid embarrassing counterparts in front of their team. The fifth foundation is legal and institutional literacy. Know the applicable law, the arbitration venue, and the enforcement reality. The New York Convention on the Recognition and Enforcement of Foreign Arbitral Awards has many African signatories, but enforcement still varies. Regional courts, OHADA in West and Central Africa, and the AfCFTA dispute settlement mechanism are relevant. Understand Incoterms 2020, UCP 600 for letters of credit, CISG if applicable, and local import-export licensing. A deal that cannot be enforced is not a deal. The sixth foundation is financial engineering. African trade is often constrained by foreign exchange shortages, high interest rates, and limited trade finance. Negotiators must be creative: use confirmed letters of credit from a strong bank, use warehouse receipts, use export credit agencies, use factoring, use supply chain finance, or use countertrade and offset arrangements. Currency choice matters. If you price in USD but your costs are in naira or birr, you carry exchange risk. If you price in local currency, your buyer may resist. Solutions include currency clauses, forward contracts, natural hedging by buying inputs in the same currency, and splitting the difference. The seventh foundation is logistics and border reality. A great price with a two-month delay at the port is a bad deal. Know the corridor: Mombasa to Kampala, Durban to Lusaka, Lagos to Niamey, Tanger Med to Europe, Djibouti to Addis. Know the border posts, the customs systems such as ASYCUDA, the single window platforms, the weighbridge rules, and the informal costs. Build buffer time into delivery commitments. Use Incoterms that match your capacity. If you cannot control transport, do not accept DAP or DDP. The eighth foundation is negotiation process discipline. Prepare, open, explore, propose, bargain, close, and document. In preparation, define interests, not just positions. In opening, anchor reasonably with justification. In exploration, ask questions and listen. In proposing, offer packages with trade-offs. In bargaining, concede slowly and only for something in return. In closing, summarize verbally and confirm in writing. In documentation, use a term sheet, then a contract, then a purchase order, then a letter of credit. The ninth foundation is ethics and reputation. African trade has suffered from scams, fake documents, and non-performing buyers and sellers. Protect yourself with verification: company registration checks, bank references, trade references, site visits, and third-party inspection. Be trustworthy yourself. Reputation is the cheapest form of trade finance. The tenth foundation is continuous learning. Track AfCFTA implementation, tariff phase-downs, rules of origin, and new corridors such as the Lobito Corridor. Track currency policies in Nigeria, Egypt, Ethiopia, Ghana, and Kenya. Track shipping rates and container availability. The negotiator who learns fastest wins the most. In summary, foreign trade negotiation in Africa is not just haggling over price. It is a system of preparation, intelligence, cultural fluency, legal awareness, financial creativity, logistics realism, process discipline, ethics, and learning. Master these foundations and you will negotiate better deals, build stronger partnerships, and contribute to Africa's growing role in global trade.

lessons.title: Preparation, Research, and Mandate Setting for African Trade Deals
lessons.body: Preparation is where most African trade negotiations are won or lost. A negotiator who arrives without a mandate, without market data, and without a fallback plan is not negotiating; they are reacting. This lesson gives you a practical preparation system you can use for any cross-border deal, whether you are exporting cashew from Tanzania, importing pharmaceuticals into Kenya, sourcing textiles from Morocco, or negotiating a distribution agreement in Senegal. Step one is to define the deal type. Is it a one-off spot sale, a recurring supply contract, an agency or distribution agreement, a joint venture, a licensing arrangement, or a government procurement tender. Each type has different preparation needs. A spot sale needs price, quality, and payment certainty. A supply contract needs volume commitments, price adjustment formulas, and performance guarantees. An agency agreement needs territory, exclusivity, commission, and termination clauses. A joint venture needs capital, governance, intellectual property, and exit provisions. A tender needs compliance, bid bonds, and local content. Step two is to build a country and counterparty profile. For the country, collect GDP, population, import-export statistics, currency regime, inflation, political calendar, trade agreements, tariff structure, and logistics performance index. For the counterparty, collect legal name, registration number, ownership, years in business, bank references, trade references, litigation history, and reputation in the industry. Use embassy trade offices, chambers of commerce, export promotion agencies, credit rating agencies, and industry networks. In Africa, personal verification matters. Ask a trusted contact in the market to visit the buyer's office. Check whether the address is real, whether the warehouse exists, and whether the team is professional. Step three is to analyze the product and the HS code. The HS code determines duty, regulatory requirements, and eligibility for trade preferences. If you are exporting under AfCFTA, AGOA, EU EPA, or COMESA preferences, you must meet rules of origin. That may require local content, certificate of origin, and supply chain documentation. A wrong HS code can cost you money, delay clearance, or trigger penalties. Step four is to calculate your cost and price floor. Build a landed cost model for imports and an export cost model for exports. Include ex-works cost, packaging, inland transport, port charges, customs brokerage, freight, insurance, duties, VAT, bank charges, and currency conversion. Add a risk premium for delay, damage, and non-payment. Your walk-away price is not your cost; it is your cost plus the minimum acceptable margin plus risk. Write it down and do not cross it without a formal mandate review. Step five is to define your interests and their interests. Positions are what you say you want. Interests are why you want it. A buyer may say the price is too high. The interest may be cash flow, budget approval, or competitive pressure. A seller may say delivery is impossible. The interest may be production capacity, raw material availability, or shipping schedule. When you understand interests, you can create options: different payment terms, different volumes, different delivery windows, different quality grades, different packaging, different contract length. Step six is to map the stakeholders. In African trade, the person at the table may not be the decision maker. There may be a technical committee, a finance director, a customs agent, a regulator, a family owner, or a government official. Map who influences, who decides, who blocks, and who benefits. Prepare messages for each. Step seven is to choose your negotiation team and roles. A good team has a lead negotiator, a technical expert, a finance expert, and a note-taker. The lead speaks. The technical expert answers specification questions. The finance expert handles payment and currency. The note-taker records concessions and action items. Agree on signals before the meeting. Never let two people give different answers. Step eight is to prepare your opening, your concessions, and your closing. Your opening should be ambitious but justifiable. Use objective criteria: market price, cost breakdown, industry standard, previous contract. Your concession plan should list what you can give, in what order, and what you want in return. Never give a concession for free. Your closing plan should include a term sheet, a timeline, and a signature authority. Step nine is to prepare for risk. Identify currency risk, payment risk, performance risk, political risk, regulatory risk, and logistics risk. For each, decide mitigation: advance payment, letter of credit, credit insurance, hedging, dual sourcing, buffer stock, force majeure clause, arbitration clause, and exit clause. Step ten is to prepare the logistics. Confirm port of loading and discharge, transit time, shipping line, container availability, customs broker, inspection requirement, and documentation. In Africa, port congestion, border delays, and documentation errors are common. Build a timeline with buffers. Confirm who handles what under the chosen Incoterm. Step eleven is to prepare the legal framework. Decide governing law, arbitration seat, language, and dispute resolution. Consider OHADA, English common law, French civil law, or Sharia law depending on the jurisdiction. Check whether the counterparty's country is a signatory to the New York Convention. Check whether there is a bilateral investment treaty. Step twelve is to prepare the negotiation logistics. Choose a neutral venue if possible. Confirm interpretation if needed. Prepare printed and digital copies of documents. Test internet connectivity for virtual meetings. Set an agenda and share it in advance. Start with easy items to build momentum. Step thirteen is to prepare a BATNA, your best alternative to a negotiated agreement. If you are an exporter and the buyer refuses your price, what will you do. Sell to another buyer, process the raw material, store it, or sell domestically. A strong BATNA gives you confidence. A weak BATNA means you must improve your alternatives before negotiating. Step fourteen is to prepare a negotiation journal. Record assumptions, questions, data sources, and unknowns. After the meeting, record what was said, what was agreed, and what was deferred. This becomes institutional memory. Step fifteen is to prepare a mandate review checkpoint. Before you concede anything major, pause and check against the mandate. If the deal requires going beyond the mandate, escalate to the decision maker. Do not improvise on price, payment, or exclusivity. In practice, preparation for African trade deals often takes longer than the negotiation itself. That is normal. The negotiator who has done the work can move quickly because they know their numbers, their alternatives, and their limits. The negotiator who has not done the work will either lose money or lose the deal. Use this lesson as a checklist. Build a standard preparation template for your organization. Update it for each market. Train your team. Over time, preparation becomes a competitive advantage.

lessons.title: Communication, Culture, and Relationship Building Across African Markets
lessons.body: Communication is the engine of foreign trade negotiation. In Africa, communication is also the bridge between different business cultures, languages, and expectations. A negotiator who masters communication and culture can turn a difficult deal into a long-term partnership. A negotiator who ignores them can lose a profitable contract over a misunderstood word or an unintended insult. This lesson gives you practical tools for communicating and building relationships across African markets. Start with language. Africa has thousands of languages, but business is conducted in English, French, Portuguese, Arabic, Swahili, and increasingly Amharic, Hausa, Yoruba, Igbo, Zulu, and others. If you are negotiating in a second language, speak clearly, avoid idioms, and confirm understanding. If you are negotiating through an interpreter, speak in short segments, look at the counterparty not the interpreter, and allow time for translation. Provide written summaries in the counterparty's preferred language. In francophone Africa, a French-language contract may be legally required. In lusophone Africa, Portuguese is essential. In North Africa, Arabic and French are common. Do not assume that English is enough. Next, understand high-context and low-context communication. Many African business cultures are high-context: meaning is carried by tone, timing, silence, body language, and relationship, not only by words. A direct no may be softened. A maybe may mean no. A yes may mean I heard you, not I agree. Low-context cultures, such as Germany, the Netherlands, and the United States, rely on explicit written communication. When these cultures meet, misunderstanding is common. The practical solution is to use both: build relationship in person, then confirm every important point in writing. Ask clarifying questions. Say what you understood and ask if it is correct. Use phrases such as please help me understand, what would need to be true for this to work, and if I hear you correctly, you are saying. This reduces ambiguity without causing embarrassment. Relationship building is not a delay; it is an investment. In many African markets, people buy from people they trust. Trust is built through shared meals, visits, introductions, and consistency. Accept hospitality when offered. Offer it in return. Learn a few words of greeting in the local language. Ask about family, health, and business in a respectful way. Be patient with small talk. Do not rush to the contract. At the same time, be professional. Arrive on time, dress appropriately, bring business cards, and follow up. Respect hierarchy. In many African contexts, age and seniority carry authority. Greet the most senior person first. Do not contradict a senior person publicly. If you must disagree, do it privately or through a trusted intermediary. Use titles such as Chief, Dr, Engineer, Honorable, or Mr and Mrs. In some cultures, first names are used only after a relationship is established. Observe and mirror. Understand the role of time. In some contexts, time is flexible and relationships matter more than schedules. In others, especially in South Africa, Kenya, and North Africa, punctuality is expected. Ask your local contact about the norm. Build buffer time into your agenda. Do not show frustration if a meeting starts late. Use the waiting time to build relationships. Understand negotiation styles. Some cultures are competitive and assertive. Others are collaborative and consensus-seeking. Some use silence as a tactic. Others use rapid concessions to build goodwill. Some prefer to negotiate in a group. Others prefer one-on-one. Adapt your style without losing your substance. If you are a direct negotiator, soften your delivery. If you are an indirect negotiator, state your position clearly at the right moment. Use objective criteria to bridge differences. Understand the role of intermediaries. In many African markets, deals are facilitated by brokers, agents, community leaders, or government officials. A good intermediary can open doors, verify credibility, and resolve disputes. A bad intermediary can distort information and create dependency. Choose intermediaries carefully. Agree on fees, scope, and exclusivity. Keep direct communication with the principal. Do not let the intermediary become the only channel. Understand gift-giving and hospitality. In some cultures, small gifts are a normal part of relationship building. In others, they may be seen as inappropriate. Know the law. Many African countries have anti-bribery and anti-corruption laws, and foreign companies may also be subject to the US Foreign Corrupt Practices Act or the UK Bribery Act. Never offer or accept anything that could be interpreted as a bribe. Instead, invest in legitimate relationship building: training, site visits, joint planning, and community projects. Understand conflict and face-saving. In many African cultures, preserving dignity is important. Public criticism can damage a relationship permanently. If a problem arises, address it privately. Use indirect language. Offer a face-saving solution. If you need to reject a proposal, reject the proposal, not the person. Say that the proposal does not work for you, and propose an alternative. Understand decision-making. In some cultures, decisions are made at the top. In others, they are made by consensus. In family-owned businesses, the founder may decide. In state-owned enterprises, committees and political considerations matter. In multinationals, regional and global headquarters may be involved. Map the decision process early. Ask who else needs to be consulted. Ask what the timeline is. Do not assume that the person you are meeting is the decision maker. Understand virtual communication. Since COVID-19, many African trade negotiations happen on Zoom, Teams, or WhatsApp. Virtual meetings require extra care. Test your technology. Use good lighting and clear audio. Share documents in advance. Speak slowly. Pause for questions. Confirm understanding more often. Follow up with a written summary. Be aware of time zones. Be aware of data costs and connectivity issues. Offer to send a voice note or a short video if that helps. Understand written communication. Email is common but not universal. WhatsApp is widely used for quick coordination. Contracts must be formal. Use clear language. Avoid slang and idioms. Number your points. Use tables for price, volume, and delivery. Confirm receipt. Keep a record of all communications. Understand negotiation ethics. Trust is the foundation of African trade. If you make a promise, keep it. If you cannot, communicate early. If you make a mistake, admit it and fix it. Reputation travels fast in African business networks. A single bad deal can close many doors. A single good deal can open many. In summary, communication and culture are not soft skills in African trade negotiation. They are core commercial skills. Learn the languages, read the context, build the relationships, respect the hierarchy, manage the time, adapt the style, use intermediaries wisely, avoid corruption, protect dignity, map decisions, master virtual tools, write clearly, and act ethically. Do these things and you will negotiate not just a contract, but a partnership that lasts.

lessons.title: Structuring the Deal: Price, Payment, Delivery, and Risk Allocation
lessons.body: A foreign trade deal is a package of terms. Price is the most visible term, but payment, delivery, quality, and risk allocation often determine whether the deal makes or loses money. This lesson shows you how to structure a trade deal for African markets, with practical examples and checklists. Start with price. Price is not a single number. It is a combination of unit price, currency, volume, quality, Incoterm, payment terms, and contract duration. A lower unit price with open account payment may be worse than a higher unit price with a confirmed letter of credit. A higher price with DDP delivery may be worse than a lower price with FOB if you cannot manage customs and transport. Always calculate the total landed cost or total export revenue. Use a price formula when possible. For commodities, link the price to a reference such as the London Metal Exchange, the ICE futures price, or a published index. For manufactured goods, use a cost-plus formula with a margin. For services, use a day rate or a milestone-based fee. Include a price adjustment clause for currency, fuel, or raw material changes. Define the currency. In African trade, USD, EUR, and CNY are common. Local currencies are used for domestic sales and sometimes for regional trade. If you price in a foreign currency but your costs are local, you carry currency risk. Mitigate with forward contracts, natural hedging, or a currency sharing clause. Define the Incoterm. Incoterms 2020 defines who pays for transport, insurance, customs, and risk. FOB means the seller delivers to the port and the buyer takes over from there. CIF means the seller pays freight and insurance to the destination port. DAP means the seller delivers to a named place, with the buyer handling import customs. DDP means the seller handles everything, including import duties. Choose the Incoterm that matches your capacity and risk appetite. If you are a small African exporter, FOB or FCA is often safer. If you are a large importer with a customs broker, DAP may work. Never accept DDP in a country where you cannot clear goods. Define quality and specification. Use international standards such as ISO, Codex, or industry-specific standards. Define moisture, purity, size, packaging, labeling, and certification. Agree on inspection. Use a third-party inspection company such as SGS, Bureau Veritas, or Cotecna. Define the inspection point, the inspection method, and who pays. A pre-shipment inspection certificate can prevent disputes. Define payment terms. The main options are advance payment, letter of credit, documentary collection, open account, and escrow. Advance payment is safest for the seller but difficult for the buyer. Letter of credit is common in African trade but can be expensive and document-heavy. Use a confirmed irrevocable LC from a reputable bank. Check the LC terms carefully. Avoid discrepancies. Documentary collection, such as D/P or D/A, is cheaper but riskier. Open account is common with trusted long-term buyers but requires credit insurance or factoring. Escrow and fintech platforms are growing in Africa. Mobile money is useful for small transactions but not for large trade deals. Define the payment schedule. For a supply contract, use milestones: deposit, pre-shipment, post-shipment, and retention. For a project, use progress payments. For a distribution agreement, use minimum order quantities and credit limits. Define risk allocation. Who bears the risk of loss, damage, delay, non-payment, currency fluctuation, political instability, and force majeure. Use insurance. Cargo insurance is essential. Credit insurance protects against buyer default. Political risk insurance protects against expropriation, war, and transfer restrictions. Use guarantees. A bank guarantee or performance bond can secure performance. A parent company guarantee can secure a subsidiary. Use force majeure clauses that are specific and practical. Include pandemics, strikes, port closures, border closures, currency inconvertibility, and government action. Define dispute resolution. Choose arbitration over litigation when possible. Common venues include the ICC, LCIA, AFSA, and the Cairo Regional Centre for International Commercial Arbitration. For African deals, consider the OHADA Common Court of Justice and Arbitration, the COMESA Court of Justice, and the AfCFTA dispute settlement mechanism. Define the governing law. English law, French law, and New York law are common. Local law may be required for certain contracts. Define the language. If there is a conflict between languages, state which version prevails. Define the term and termination. For a supply contract, define the initial term, renewal, and termination for convenience or cause. For an agency agreement, define territory, exclusivity, commission, and post-termination obligations. For a joint venture, define capital, governance, profit sharing, and exit. Define confidentiality and intellectual property. Protect your trademarks, patents, and trade secrets. Use non-disclosure agreements before sharing sensitive information. Define the data protection rules if personal data is involved. Define compliance. Include anti-bribery, sanctions, export control, and environmental and social clauses. Many African countries have local content requirements. Check them. Define the documentation. A typical African trade deal includes a proforma invoice, a sales contract, a purchase order, a commercial invoice, a packing list, a bill of lading or airway bill, a certificate of origin, an inspection certificate, an insurance certificate, and a bank letter of credit. Each document must be accurate and consistent. A small error can delay payment or clearance. Define the logistics. Choose the route, the carrier, the port, and the customs broker. Confirm transit time and buffer. Confirm container availability and shipping schedule. Confirm border opening hours and customs systems. Confirm whether the destination port has congestion. Confirm whether the destination country has import restrictions or quotas. Define the relationship governance. Agree on communication channels, meeting frequency, performance review, and escalation. Appoint a relationship manager on each side. Use a scorecard for quality, delivery, and payment. In practice, structuring an African trade deal requires iteration. Start with a term sheet. Negotiate the big items first: price, payment, delivery, and risk. Then negotiate the details: quality, inspection, documentation, and dispute resolution. Use a lawyer and a customs broker. Use a banker for payment instruments. Use an insurer for risk. Do not sign a contract you do not understand. Do not accept terms you cannot perform. Do not rely on verbal promises. Write everything down. A well-structured deal is not the one with the highest price. It is the one that is bankable, insurable, shippable, and enforceable. That is the deal that creates repeat business and builds Africa's trade future.

lessons.title: Closing, Documentation, and Post-Deal Management in African Trade
lessons.body: Closing a foreign trade negotiation is not the end. It is the beginning of performance. In African trade, many deals fail not because the negotiation was bad, but because the closing and post-deal management were weak. This lesson covers how to close, document, and manage a trade deal so that it delivers value and leads to repeat business. Start with the closing conversation. When the main terms are agreed, summarize them verbally. Confirm each item: product, quantity, quality, price, currency, Incoterm, payment terms, delivery date, inspection, documentation, and dispute resolution. Ask the counterparty to confirm. Then say that you will send a written summary. Do not leave the meeting without a clear next step and a timeline. Use a term sheet or a memorandum of understanding. A term sheet is a short document that captures the agreed commercial terms. It is usually non-binding except for confidentiality and exclusivity. A memorandum of understanding is broader and may be binding or non-binding depending on the language. Both are useful because they prevent later disputes about what was agreed. Keep the term sheet simple. Use bullet points. Number the items. Include the date and the names of the parties. Then move to the contract. The contract is the binding document. It should be written by a lawyer who knows the applicable law and the trade sector. Do not copy a template from the internet without adapting it. The contract should include the parties, the recitals, the definitions, the scope, the price, the payment, the delivery, the quality, the inspection, the risk, the insurance, the term, the termination, the confidentiality, the intellectual property, the compliance, the force majeure, the dispute resolution, the governing law, the notices, and the signatures. Use clear language. Avoid ambiguity. Define key terms. Use schedules and annexes for specifications, price lists, and delivery schedules. In African trade, some contracts must be registered or notarized. Check the local requirements. Some countries require a local agent or a local bank. Check the import-export regulations. Some products require a license or a permit. Check the food, drug, agricultural, and hazardous materials rules. Once the contract is signed, move to execution. Issue the proforma invoice. Confirm the letter of credit. Book the freight. Arrange the inspection. Prepare the documents. Coordinate with the customs broker. Confirm the shipping schedule. Communicate with the buyer at every stage. Do not disappear after signing. The buyer needs to know that you are reliable. Use a shipment checklist. The checklist should include the commercial invoice, the packing list, the bill of lading or airway bill, the certificate of origin, the inspection certificate, the insurance certificate, the fumigation certificate if needed, the phytosanitary certificate if needed, the health certificate if needed, and the bank documents. Check every document for accuracy. The name of the buyer, the name of the seller, the description of the goods, the quantity, the price, the port, the vessel, and the date must match. A discrepancy can delay payment or clearance. Use a document tracker. Record when each document is prepared, checked, sent, and received. Use a payment tracker. Record when the deposit is received, when the LC is opened, when the documents are presented, and when the balance is paid. Follow up on overdue payments. Use a polite but firm approach. Escalate if necessary. Use credit insurance or a collections agency if the buyer defaults. Manage logistics. Track the shipment. Confirm the vessel departure and arrival. Confirm the customs clearance. Confirm the delivery to the buyer's warehouse. If there is a delay, communicate early. Offer a solution. Do not hide problems. Manage quality. If the buyer complains, investigate. Use the inspection report. Use photos and videos. If the product is defective, replace it or compensate. Protect your reputation. Manage the relationship. After delivery, ask for feedback. Ask for a testimonial. Ask for a repeat order. Ask for a referral. Visit the buyer if possible. Attend trade fairs. Send updates on new products and prices. Celebrate milestones. Build trust over time. Manage performance. Use a scorecard. Track on-time delivery, quality, payment, and communication. Review the scorecard with the buyer every quarter. Discuss improvements. Discuss new opportunities. Discuss risks. Manage risk continuously. Monitor currency, political, regulatory, and logistics risks. Update your contracts and insurance. Diversify your buyers and suppliers. Keep a contingency plan. Manage documentation for the long term. Keep copies of all contracts, invoices, bills of lading, certificates, and correspondence. Store them digitally and physically. Keep them for the legally required period. Use them for audits, tax, and dispute resolution. Manage disputes. If a dispute arises, try to resolve it amicably first. Use the escalation clause. Use mediation. Use arbitration if necessary. Do not let a small dispute destroy a valuable relationship. Manage learning. After each deal, conduct a debrief. What went well. What went wrong. What would you do differently. Update your preparation template, your contract template, and your checklist. Train your team. Share the lessons. In African trade, closing and post-deal management are where reputations are built. A negotiator who signs a contract but cannot deliver will not get a second chance. A negotiator who delivers on time, communicates clearly, and solves problems will get repeat business and referrals. That is how African businesses grow from local traders to regional players to global competitors. Use this lesson as a guide. Close carefully. Document thoroughly. Manage proactively. Learn continuously. Your next deal will be better because of it.

quiz.q: In foreign trade negotiation, what is the primary purpose of a letter of intent?
options: A) To legally bind both parties to final contract terms
B) To outline preliminary commitments before a formal contract
C) To replace a bill of lading in shipping
quiz.explanation: A letter of intent expresses preliminary intentions and is generally non-binding, helping parties align before drafting a formal contract.

quiz.q: Which Incoterm places the most responsibility on the seller for delivery and costs?
quiz.explanation: DDP (Delivered Duty Paid) requires the seller to bear all costs and risks, including import duties, until the goods reach the buyer.

quiz.q: What is a common negotiation tactic when the counterparty uses a deadline as pressure?
options: B) Accept immediately to avoid risk
C) Test the deadline validity and propose a mutual timeline
quiz.explanation: Testing whether a deadline is real and proposing a mutually acceptable timeline reduces pressure and keeps dialogue constructive.

quiz.q: In cross-cultural trade negotiation, what does high-context communication typically rely on?
options: D) Implicit cues, relationships, and shared understanding
quiz.explanation: High-context cultures rely on implicit cues, relationships, and shared background rather than explicit verbal statements.

quiz.q: Which document is most important for verifying the origin of goods to claim preferential tariffs?
quiz.explanation: A certificate of origin confirms where goods were produced, which is required to claim preferential tariff treatment under trade agreements.

quiz.q: What is the best response when a foreign buyer demands a price reduction after agreement?
options: A) Immediately accept to preserve the relationship
B) Review the contract terms and offer non-price concessions if needed
C) Threaten legal action without discussion
quiz.explanation: Reviewing contract terms and offering non-price concessions, such as payment or delivery flexibility, can preserve value and the relationship.

quiz.q: Which payment method offers the seller the highest security in international trade?
quiz.explanation: An irrevocable letter of credit provides a bank guarantee, giving the seller strong assurance of payment if documents comply.

quiz.q: During a trade negotiation, what does BATNA stand for?
options: A) Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement
B) Bilateral Agreement on Tariffs and Negotiation
C) Basic Assessment of Trade and Needs
D) Binding Arbitration Terms and Notices
quiz.explanation: BATNA means Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement, the fallback option if no deal is reached, which shapes negotiating power.
